1.patternText: Jacob dwells in Canaan where his father sojourned; Joseph, seventeen years old, shepherds the flock and receives a variegated tunic from his father.
patternRows: Κατῴκει δὲ Ἰακὼβ ἐν τῇ γῇ

rules.title: κατοικεῖν vs. παροικεῖν
rules.rule: κατοικεῖν here signifies a more permanent residence than παροικεῖν. Jacob dwelt where Abraham only sojourned. From meaning a settlement of Jews in a foreign country, παροικία came to mean an ecclesiastical district or diocese — the origin of our word parish.

rules.title: Analytic Imperfect (ἦν ποιμαίνων)
rules.rule: ἦν ποιμαίνων is the analytic (periphrastic) form of the imperfect = ἐποίμαινε. Such forms occur in all stages of the language and are especially common in the LXX and N.T.

rules.title: Comparison with παρά (παρὰ πάντας)
rules.rule: παρὰ πάντας means more than all. The Hebrew language has no comparative degree of adjectives, and the LXX frequently expresses comparison by παρά or ἐκ with the positive.

rules.title: ἐκ πάντων = παρὰ πάντας
rules.rule: ἐκ πάντων in v. 4 is a different rendering of the same Hebrew original as παρὰ πάντας in v. 3, both expressing the comparative: more than all.

rules.title: Cognate Accusative (ἐνυπνιασθεὶς ἐνύπνιον)
rules.rule: A verb may take an accusative noun of kindred meaning (cognate accusative): ἐνυπνιασθεὶς ἐνύπνιον, having dreamed a dream. This Greek idiom closely matches the Hebrew.

rules.title: Genitive After ἀκούω
rules.rule: ἀκούω (I hear) regularly takes the genitive of the sound or speech heard: ἀκούσατε τοῦ ἐνυπνίου τούτου (hear this dream).

rules.title: Participle + Finite Verb (βασιλεύων βασιλεύσεις)
rules.rule: The LXX renders the Hebrew infinitive absolute by a participle of the same verb: βασιλεύων βασιλεύσεις (shalt thou indeed reign), ἐλθόντες ἐλευσόμεθα (shall we indeed come).

rules.title: Hebraism: προσέθεντο ἔτι μισεῖν
rules.rule: προσέθεντο ἔτι μισεῖν literally means they added yet to hate = they hated him still more — a Hebraism very common throughout the LXX.

rules.title: Echo in the New Testament (v. 11)
rules.rule: ὁ δὲ πατὴρ αὐτοῦ διετήρησε τὸ ῥῆμα (his father kept the saying): Luke 2:19 and 2:51 (Mary kept all these sayings in her heart) are modelled directly on this Septuagint verse.

rules.rule: The LXX frequently reflects Hebrew syntax in Greek dress: παρά/ἐκ for comparison (παρὰ πάντας), participle + finite verb for emphasis (βασιλεύων βασιλεύσεις), and προστίθημι + infinitive for “again / still more” (προσέθεντο ἔτι μισεῖν).

rules.title: Analytic Imperfect & Imperatives
rules.rule: ἦν + present participle (ἦν ποιμαίνων) serves as an analytic imperfect; 3rd plural imperatives regularly end in -ωσαν (ἔστωσαν).

rules.title: Classical Constructions Retained
rules.rule: Alongside Hebraisms, the Pentateuch preserves idiomatic Greek: genitive after ἀκούω, elliptical εἰς ᾅδου, vivid subjunctive ὅπως ἐξέληται, and deponent futures (καταβήσομαι).

rules.title: After is, both sides stay nominative
rules.rule: ἐστίν means is, the present of the same verb as ἦν, was. The pattern does not change: the subject and the predicate — the word that tells what the subject is — both stay in the nominative.
rules.because: ἐστίν does not take an object. ἀγάπη is the predicate, so it stays nominative, like θεός after ἦν in John 1:1.

rules.title: The article still marks the subject
rules.rule: With ἐστίν, as with ἦν, the noun that has the article is the subject. The predicate often has no article.
rules.because: ὁ θεός is the subject, God. φῶς is the predicate, light, and stays nominative.
